articles.title: Attacks on Saudi oil expose Iraqi PM’s struggle to control armed factions
articles.summary: A senior Iraqi source points to a resistance ‘splinter’ group for the September attack on the East-West pipeline.
articles.body:
As black smoke billowed over Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline, the repercussions of the drone attack were already reaching across the border into Iraq.

The strikes, launched from Iraqi territory, threatened about 4 percent of global oil supplies and helped push Brent crude above $108 a barrel. But they also presented Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi with perhaps the clearest test yet of his pledge to bring armed groups under state control as the US-led coalition is due to make its final withdrawal by September 30.

No group has claimed responsibility for the attacks launched last Thursday. The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella of pro-Iranian factions including Kataib Hezbollah, has denied involvement, calling the strike “an honour that we do not claim”.

Baghdad has confirmed the drones came from Iraqi soil. Security forces identified launch traces near the Duwayrij River in Maysan province’s al-Tayeb border area on Saturday. Lieutenant General Saad Maan, head of Iraq’s Security Media Cell, said an intelligence task force had seized a launch platform.

A senior source at the Ministry of Interior told Al Jazeera he believed a resistance splinter group was responsible, though this has not been confirmed. If true, it points to a deeper problem: factions operating outside the state’s chain of command, and subgroups that operate outside the factions’ control.

Michael Knights, a research lead at Washington-based consultancy Horizon Engage, was sceptical, noting that front groups are an old ploy to make reluctant governments think twice before retaliating.

He said it was probably a cell run directly by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) or one of the established armed factions. “They just want to make it marginally harder for anyone to pin it on them,” he said.

Under international pressure, Zaidi has responded quickly. He sacked the Maysan operations commander, ordered the formation of an investigative committee to look into the incident and closed numerous border crossings with Iran to prevent perpetrators from fleeing. In a visual display, heavily armed troops in Humvees appeared on Maysan’s streets.

But to many observers, such moves are just a show to placate Saudi and US calls for action, as the September attack was not the first originating from Iraqi soil.

In July, drones launched from Iraq struck Saudi oil facilities, reportedly with help from Houthi fighters based in Iraq. The US and Saudi Arabia retaliated with strikes that killed more than 20 members of Iraq’s Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), including Iranian military advisers. The resulting diplomatic fallout forced al-Zaidi to postpone a planned trip to Riyadh.

The violence is threatening to undermine Iraq and Saudi Arabia’s warming relations. Riyadh froze ties after Iraq’s 1990 invasion of Kuwait, re-engaging in the mid-2010s as ISIL rose. Border crossings reopened in 2020, and talk has since turned to investment, electricity links and transport. Saudi intelligence chief Khalid al-Humaidan visited Baghdad this month, and Riyadh has held off retaliating against the September 10 attack at Zaidi’s request.

Lahib Higel, deputy director for the Middle East and North Africa at the International Crisis Group, said the strike may also have been a message to al-Zaidi, who has pursued greater engagement with Saudi Arabia as part of a wider strategy to diversify Iraq’s economy.

“What he’s doing with the Saudis now, I think they would be seriously concerned about,” she said of the factions, some of which have said avenging fighters killed in Saudi strikes matters more than business deals. More broadly, for fear of losing leverage, Iran and its associated factions do not want to see Iraq become less economically reliant on Tehran, or establish alternative oil export routes other than Hormuz.

Zaidi has attempted to balance relations with his neighbours, receiving Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf in August just shy of a month after the Iraqi Prime Minister made an official visit to Tehran, where he met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.

The balancing act has put the prime minister, a multimillionaire business figure who was considered a compromise candidate of the governing Shia bloc, under pressure despite reportedly being a preferred option for the US.

Zaidi’s stated intent is clear. He has ordered Iraqi banks to enforce US sanctions on Lebanon’s Hezbollah, asked parliament to draft a law to put weapons under the control of the state, and said those who refuse to disarm will be tried for treason.

But enforcement has repeatedly been thwarted. In July, troops sent to search Harakat al-Nujaba’s compound south of Baghdad were turned away with warning shots. In August, counterterrorism forces arrested Abbas al-Yaqoubi, a senior Nujaba intelligence official, only for a judge to free him 48 hours later.

However, a Baghdad court did jail a Kataib Hezbollah member for 15 years over the March kidnapping of US journalist Shelly Kittleson.

Higel said Zaidi had been bolder than former prime ministers, and that such verdicts make low-level fighters ask whether an operation is “worth 15 years”.

“But in the bigger picture, this has essentially no meaningful impact,” she said. “It’s not a system that is changing.”

Three factions – Kataib Hezbollah, Nujaba and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada – still refuse to disarm. Very few observers of Iraqi politics believe any meaningful concessions will be made, and the state has shown no sign it is willing to face off with the pro-Iranian factions.

For Knights, whether the state can act is less about firepower than nerve.

He points out that attacking Saudi Arabia was the move most likely to draw US attention back onto faction leaders – but they did it anyway. “That says to me [the armed factions] are completely fearless right now.”

Knights believes that Iraq’s Counter Terrorism Service (CTS) had the operational capability to take out the leaders of most of Iraq’s armed factions if it had the support of Iraq’s leadership, Washington and its Gulf neighbours.

But few officials have faith in the US coming to Iraq’s support, if needed. As Saudi Arabia’s call for US assistance fighting the Houthis in Yemen has reportedly gone unheeded, Baghdad may be doubtful Washington would come to its aid if the Green Zone, Iraq’s fortified government district, was besieged by resistance factions.

“This is all about confidence and feeling like your partners have your back and nobody feels like that right now,” he said.

Higel said the factions believe time is on their side and can wait out Trump. The objective for al-Zaidi may be to appear bold enough to keep Washington and Riyadh happy without provoking a backlash that could topple his government, or worse.

“I wouldn’t put it past these groups to assassinate a prime minister if it came to it,” she said.

articles.title: DRC-Rwanda: Can Geneva talks break the cycle of war in eastern Congo?
articles.summary: M23 controls large parts of eastern DRC as Kinshasa and Kigali remain divided over security and sovereignty.
articles.body:
Goma, DR Congo – More than a year after the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Rwanda signed an agreement intended to end their confrontation, the two countries are back at the negotiating table in Geneva. In eastern Congo, however, the guns have not gone quiet.

The dispute over the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), Rwanda’s military presence in Congolese territory and M23’s control of large parts of the east is now difficult to separate. While the DRC and Rwanda negotiate in Geneva, Kinshasa is pursuing a separate dialogue with the political alliance backing M23.

The talks are separate, but the conflicts they are trying to contain are not.

In Goma, where M23 fighters captured the city in January 2025, the latest round of diplomacy is being judged against what has happened since.

For Josue Akuzwe Walayi, a pro-democracy activist speaking from Kinshasa, another round of talks will mean little unless people begin to see a change in their daily lives.

“People are still waiting for the real benefits of peace that have been trumpeted for over a year. Fields continue to be ravaged in the east, and further displacement is still being reported,” he told Al Jazeera.

Why are Kinshasa and Kigali still divided?

At the heart of the dispute is the FDLR.

The armed group emerged from the aftermath of the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda, when members of the former Rwandan army and fighter groups involved in the killings fled into what is now eastern DRC. Kigali has long regarded the group’s presence near Rwanda’s border as a security threat.

Under the Washington framework, Kinshasa agreed to a process aimed at neutralising the FDLR. The Congolese government says that process, including demobilisation measures, is under way.

But Rwandan President Paul Kagame described the agreement on the FDLR as “insufficient” in remarks at the end of last month.

Patrick Muyaya, the Congolese minister of information and government spokesperson, rejected that assessment, saying Kinshasa is meeting its commitments while accusing Kigali of maintaining “expansionist ambitions” in eastern DRC.

“The work of neutralising the FDLR through demobilisation is being carried out in accordance with the Washington agreements,” Muyaya told Al Jazeera.

The disagreement is not simply over whether the FDLR process is sufficient. It reflects a deeper dispute over security and sovereignty.

Rwanda wants credible assurances that armed groups hostile to it will not operate from Congolese territory. Kinshasa argues that Rwanda’s security concerns cannot justify the presence of foreign forces on Congolese soil.

What Rwanda sees as a necessary security measure, Kinshasa sees as a threat to its sovereignty.

That mistrust is now at the centre of the Geneva talks.

Where does M23 fit into the peace process?

M23 is not a party to the Washington agreement, but it is central to the conflict that the agreement is supposed to help contain.

The group captured Goma in January 2025 and later took Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu, dramatically altering the balance of power in eastern DRC.

M23 operates under the political umbrella of the Congo River Alliance (AFC), which has been involved in a separate Qatar-led dialogue with Kinshasa.

The Geneva process is focused on the confrontation between the DRC and Rwanda, while the Qatar process addresses the Congolese government’s dispute with the AFC-M23 alliance.

Yet on the ground, those conflicts cannot easily be separated.

M23’s territorial control shapes Kinshasa’s calculations, while the Congolese military response affects the security environment along Rwanda’s border. Rwanda’s concerns about armed groups in eastern DRC are also bound up with its position towards M23, while Kinshasa continues to demand the withdrawal of Rwandan forces.

A settlement between Kinshasa and Kigali could reduce regional tensions, but it would not necessarily end the fighting inside eastern DRC.

The talks may be taking place on separate tracks, but what happens on one can affect the others.

What does the diplomacy look like from Goma?

In Goma, where residents have lived through repeated cycles of fighting and displacement, diplomacy is ultimately being measured against what happens outside the conference rooms.

Sadiki Bitha, a resident who experienced the city’s capture in January 2025, is following the Geneva talks and wants the parties and their mediators to ensure that their commitments are honoured.

For Walayi, the continued violence has made it difficult to view another round of diplomacy with confidence.

He accuses Rwanda of supporting violence in eastern DRC and of invoking the FDLR threat to justify its military actions.

“Rwanda prefers to attack us in order to secure its borders within our country, something we cannot accept,” he said.

“The threat posed by the FDLR cannot justify a Rwandan military presence on Congolese territory. Rwanda’s security must not, under any circumstances, be built at the expense of our country’s sovereignty.”

Rwanda rejects accusations that it is pursuing territorial expansion.

The dispute is difficult to resolve because Kinshasa and Kigali disagree over both the threat and how it should be addressed. Neither side appears ready to change its military posture without guarantees from the other.

For people in eastern DRC, however, those arguments are measured in more immediate terms: Displacement, violence and the loss of access to land and livelihoods.

Can the ceasefire hold while the accusations continue?

While the talks continue, fighting persists in North and South Kivu between the DRC army and allied armed groups and M23 fighters.

AFC-M23 has accused Kinshasa of attacking populated areas and violating the ceasefire.

“The AFC-M23 calls on the Congolese people and the international community to bear witness to these serious attacks against the civilian population, which violate the ceasefire,” Lawrence Kanyuka, spokesperson for AFC-M23, told Al Jazeera.

“The AFC-M23 will take all necessary measures to establish a security perimeter to protect these people.”

The allegations could not be independently verified.

On August 27, AFC-M23 also said an aircraft carrying humanitarian aid and essential supplies had been shot down by the DRC army and described it as a civilian aircraft.

When contacted by Al Jazeera, Mak Hazukay, acting spokesperson for the DRC army, declined to comment on the allegation.

The incident also shows how quickly a disputed event can become part of the conflict itself. Without a trusted mechanism for establishing what happened, disputed incidents can quickly become another source of confrontation.

That makes verification central to whether any ceasefire can survive.

Herve Amani, a civil society activist, believes the meeting should not be dismissed simply because previous diplomatic efforts have failed.

For him, the priority is to reduce tensions and begin rebuilding trust between the two countries.

“This meeting in Switzerland should be seen as an opportunity rather than yet another diplomatic exercise,” he told Al Jazeera.

“We must not underestimate the difficulties, but we must also recognise that dialogue remains preferable to escalation.”

Geneva will not resolve decades of mistrust between Kinshasa and Kigali. Nor will it settle M23’s position or, on its own, end the wider conflict in eastern DRC.

But it can still matter if it produces commitments that are concrete, implementable and verifiable.

For Rwanda, that means credible progress towards neutralising the FDLR and addressing its security concerns.

For the DRC, it means respect for its territorial sovereignty and progress towards the withdrawal of Rwandan forces.

And for the wider peace effort, progress on one track cannot come at the expense of the other.

For civilians caught between armed groups and national armies, however, the test is simpler: Whether the guns finally fall silent.

Bitha, who lived through the capture of Goma, says he still believes the Geneva meeting can offer a way forward.

“We have high hopes for this meeting. Every 21 September marks the International Day of Peace. We believe this is an opportunity for the people of Congo and Rwanda to speak with one voice and silence the guns by mutual agreement,” he told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: 'Might be running out of time to avoid outcome of AI killing all humans'
articles.summary: US News: A former Google DeepMind employee Monday became the latest AI researcher to warn that the technology could \"kill all humans\", saying time could be run.
articles.body: A former Google DeepMind employee Monday became the latest AI researcher to warn that the technology could "kill all humans", saying time could be running out to avoid the outcome. Public alarm about the potential danger posed by AI is growing, after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said last week he had resigned, in part because the "people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade".Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger then responded to Coxon's comments, saying he was correct and that he believed there was a greater than 10% chance that AI could kill all humans within the next decade. "I recently resigned from Google DeepMind, where I worked on AGI safety and alignment research," Bilal Chughtai wrote on X. "At Google, I witnessed AI development first hand. I too am extremely concerned by the default trajectory of this technology. I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome."Chughtai, who co-authored research papers while at Google DeepMind, worked there as a research engineer and left the company in July 2026, according to his LinkedIn profile. Google did not respond to a request for comment outside regular business hours. Chughtai also said that navigating AI safely was possible but would require coordination "to avoid this maniac race between AI companies". "We need to pace AI development to a speed that society can handle, where emerging risks can be addressed before extreme harm is realised," he added.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Mayors could be given powers to oversee water companies under government plan
articles.summary: The idea is to create nine new regional bodies responsible for planning, setting objectives and holding water companies to account.
articles.body:
Mayors and other local political leaders could be given powers to oversee water companies under plans being considered by the government.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's plan is to create nine new regional bodies responsible for planning, setting objectives, and holding water companies to account.

The idea was a key recommendation of Sir John Cunliffe's Independent Water Commission published in June last year.

Improving the water industry has been a focus for Burnham since he took to power, as water customers in England and Wales continue to face steep bill hikes.

But there has been little detail of what that could look like, short of full nationalisation - until now.

Some ideas in the Cunliffe report were adopted by Sir Keir Starmer's government, however the recommendation for regional bodies was not.

While no final decision has been made, and the timings for any announcement have not been finalised, officials in the Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs are understood to be keen on the idea.

The regional bodies would be given powers to oversee elements of water companies' spending and hold bosses to account over bills and sewage discharges.

The Cunliffe review said: "This would represent a significant change, and ensure that local voices, customers and experts have stronger authority over companies' boards' decisions on investment priorities."

As well as a mayor, or local government figure, the regional bodies could consist of an independent chair, experts, and representatives to cover affected sectors like transport and agriculture.

A Whitehall source said it was just one among a number of ideas being explored to bring greater public control of water companies.

A government spokesperson said: "Our water industry has not been working for people for far too long. We're bringing in tougher regulation, stronger enforcement and greater accountability, so water companies deliver for customers and the environment."

The Consumer Council for Water (CCW) said the year-on-year increase was the highest in its 20-year history and showed "just how dissatisfied" many people were.

In recent years there has been growing public concern about sewage spills and rising bills, as well as decades of under-investment in the sector, with climate change and population growth straining it further.

Complaints to watchdog about water firms jump 84%

During his first address to the House of Commons in September, Burnham said "a series of wrong turns" since the 1980s had seen economic power in the UK privatised, before pointing to the water industry as "a leaking monument to that approach - a country run in the private rather than public interest".

Burnham has already committed to giving mayors greater control over public services such as social housing, welfare and education.

He aims to achieve this by allowing mayors more power over budgets, in a 10-year plan to transform the economy.

The prime minister said he would give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his drive to transfer power from Westminster to local leaders.

Burnham's visions come amid a backdrop of rising water prices for customers in England and Wales.

The Consumer Council for Water has said the year-on-year increase was the highest in its 20-year history.

The issue of England's water industry was also debated in Westminster on Monday after more than 200,000 people signed a petition calling for a national referendum on whether the water industry should be returned to public ownership.

While the MPs who took part in the debate did not agree with the need for a referendum, there was broad consensus that the current model was "broken", and needed to be fixed.

articles.title: Mount Fuji: Japan's Yamanashi to charge rescue fee during off season
articles.summary: The fee will be imposed on those who get lost on Japan's most famous mountain during the off-peak seasons.
articles.body:
From next year, people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service, authorities governing the northern part of the peak say.

The fee is among a series of measures Japan's Yamanashi prefecture is introducing to deter reckless and poorly prepared climbers.

A similar fee of 8,000 yen ($51; £38) per five minutes is already in place in nearby Saitama prefecture for other mountainous areas and will be used as a reference.

Yamanashi authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season, which runs from early September to July the following year, to submit detailed climbing plans.

"We ask the general public to refrain from climbing during the off-season. We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Yamanashi Governor Kotaro Nagasaki said on Monday.

Officials in Yamanashi and neighbouring Shizuoka prefecture, which governs the southern part of Fuji, have seen a rise in off-season and unplanned climbs, some of which have left climbers stranded.

Shizuoka authorities say they will impose penalties on people who fail to register their off-season climbing attempts and strengthen efforts to keep climbers out of restricted areas.

They did not announce a helicopter rescue fee.

Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from July to early September, with about 200,000 hikers attempting the summit each year.

Climbing outside of those months is highly discouraged although permitted up to the fifth of ten stations.

However, most mountain huts and toilet facilities are closed off season. The weather and trail conditions also tend to be more severe.

articles.title: Three killed in Los Angeles news helicopter crash
articles.summary: The NBCLA news helicopter was flying near the scene of a fatal bus crash.
articles.body:
Three people have died and two others taken to hospital after a news helicopter crashed in suburban Los Angeles, fire authorities in the city have said.

NBC Los Angeles confirmed the helicopter was its NewsChopper4, which also operated for Telemundo 52, and was in the area on Tuesday reporting on a deadly bus crash.

The station's hosts said both people on the helicopter, who were "valued friends and colleagues" had died, naming them as Eliana Moreno and George Marciniw.

They said the third victim was on the ground at the time of the crash, but did not name them.

The aircraft went down just before 19:00 local time (01:00 BST) between two commercial buildings in the Chatsworth neighbourhood, a Los Angeles Fire Department (LAFD) spokesperson told the BBC.

Fire from the crash spread to four vehicles and two storage containers, and more than 70 firefighters were deployed to the scene, the LAFD added.

During emotional live coverage on NBC4, veteran news anchor Colleen Williams confirmed it was the local news station's helicopter that crashed.

"We knew it was a news chopper. We knew we'd lost contact with our people out there, and we've just received confirmation," Williams said.

Earlier, LAFD Captain Branden Silverman told the local affiliate of the BBC's US partner CBS: "We do have one confirmed patient that seemed to be outside of the helicopter when it crashed.

"That person was declared deceased on scene," Silverman said.

Several news helicopters were in the area at the time of the incident reporting on a bus crash.

Earlier in the day, two people were killed and six others were injured after an SUV crashed into a city bus in Chatsworth, BBC's US partner CBS reported.

LAPD's Central Division posted on X that it extended "thoughts and prayers to the family, friends and colleagues of KNBC 4, Los Angeles".

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass wrote on X she was "absolutely devastated by the loss of life in Chatsworth tonight".

"My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we lost in the tragic bus collision and helicopter crash," she added.

California Governor Gavin Newsom wrote on X that "our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight's devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family".

"Thank you to the first responders working tirelessly tonight."

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) will lead the investigation into the incident.

articles.title: China’s defence chief warns against coercion, avoids US, Japan mention
articles.summary: Dong Jun pitches shared security governance and military cooperation while warning against coercion.
articles.body:
Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun has said that countries around the world should cease provocative acts and check the resurgence of regressive historical trends.

Dong made his remarks, likely to be taken as veiled criticism of Japan, on Wednesday while opening the 13th Beijing Xiangshan Forum. In a broad speech, he urged a fresh, more inclusive approach to resolving international tensions, though he offered few specifics or any direct criticisms of rivals.

“We must bear the lessons of history in mind and remain highly vigilant against all latent manifestations of hegemony, militarism and historical revisionism,” Dong said.

“We must not turn a blind eye or condone such behaviour. By rallying broad-based forces of justice, we must suppress the resurgence of historical dregs,” he added.

The forum is being held amid heightened regional tensions over Taiwan and the disputed South China Sea, as well as growing doubts about traditional US security commitments to Asia.

It also comes a week before an expected trip by Chinese President Xi Jinping to Washington to meet US President Donald Trump.

Dong’s address built on comments made earlier while meeting visiting foreign guests. In separate sit-downs with defence officials from Myanmar, Brunei, Belarus, Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia, as well as ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn, Dong pitched a vision of deeper military cooperation and shared security as an immediate curtain-raiser for the forum.

Over the past two decades, Beijing has carefully built the Xiangshan Forum into its primary platform for military diplomacy, positioning it as a tightly scripted alternative to Singapore’s Shangri-La Dialogue.

Bringing together hundreds of military officers, diplomats and scholars from dozens of countries, the three-day gathering provides China with a high-profile stage to champion a multipolar world and advocate for a greater voice for the Global South.

As some analysts predicted, Dong did not make direct criticisms of the United States or its regional allies, including Japan.

Ties between China and Japan plummeted after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi last year suggested a hypothetical Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger a Japanese military response, prompting repeated warnings from Beijing that Japan is seeking a return to its aggressive past.

China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has ramped up military pressure around the island, including periodically staging war games. Taiwan’s government rejects Beijing’s claims of sovereignty.

Earlier, a Chinese scholar attending the forum warned that Japan’s growing involvement in the South China Sea could undermine regional peace over the long term.

“I think that, from a longer-term perspective, Japan could be more damaging to peace and stability in the South China Sea than the United States,” Wu Shicun, chairman of the Huayang Center for Maritime Cooperation and Ocean Governance, told the Chinese news agency CNS.

Wu warned that Japan fixates on the waterway as a springboard to attack and invade Southeast Asia, and to control sea lanes. He added that Tokyo’s actions would have a series of negative effects on dispute resolution, maritime cooperation and consultations on a Code of Conduct, stressing that regional states must remain vigilant about this.

For visiting foreign envoys, navigating the forum involves balancing complex regional dynamics. Western governments have largely dispatched lower-level representatives, with the US contingent led by senior Pentagon official Cynthia Carras.

Meanwhile, neighbouring countries attempting to manage ties between Washington and Beijing sent top defence leadership, including Vietnamese Defence Minister Phan Van Giang and Malaysian Vice Defence Minister Adly Zahari. A delegation from North Korea’s Ministry of National Defence, led by Vice Minister Kim Kang Il, is also attending, according to KCNA.

articles.title: Trump administration plans $2.8bn sale of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel
articles.summary: Trump administration pushes $2.8bn bomb sale to Israel amid criticism over mass targeting of civilians in the region.
articles.body:
The Trump administration is preparing to sell Israel a $2.8bn package of 907kg (2,000-pound) bombs, the largest single sale of the munition in recent years, according to reports by the Washington Post and the AFP news agency.

The package, funded through Foreign Military Financing – a mechanism in which Washington provides the money Israel then uses to buy US weapons – includes 40,000 bombs: 20,000 MK-84 general-purpose bombs and 20,000 BLU-117s, a thermally coated variant of the MK-84 designed for safer naval storage, along with I-2000 Penetrator warheads built to strike hardened, underground structures.

According to the Post, the MK-84, nicknamed the “hammer” by US pilots in the first Gulf War, is among the most destructive munitions in Western arsenals, sending metal fragments outward for hundreds of metres and capable of tearing through thick concrete.

“An American-made Mark 84 has a destruction radius of half a mile,” conservative commentator Tucker Carlson wrote on X, citing an unnamed federal official. “It releases a thermal wave the temperature of the surface of the sun… The bomb collapses apartment buildings and leaves craters thirty-five feet deep.”

The deal has been informally notified to congressional committees.

The Post reported that a senior administration official said only that “all foreign arms sales are moving through the appropriate process,” while the State Department said it does not comment on proposed sales before formal notification to Congress.

Israel has used 907kg bombs hundreds of times in Gaza and Lebanon, including in areas it had designated safe for civilians, drawing sustained criticism from rights groups.

Former US President Joe Biden’s administration paused a single such shipment in 2024 over civilian casualty concerns – the only munition it withheld during the Gaza genocide – before Trump reversed that pause in his first month back in office.

The sale lands amid growing strain between Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and rising bipartisan unease in Washington over unconditional military support.

US Senator Chris Van Hollen said he would work to block the sale, accusing Trump of “sending bombs paid for by American taxpayers to a government led by a wanted war criminal”.

Former Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene wrote: “We did not vote for this. America does not support this. Our tax dollars and weapons have been used to kill tens of thousands of innocent people.”

Carlson called the roughly $3bn package “a gift” to the Israeli government, which is “working to exterminate an unarmed civilian population in Gaza”, calling for senators and US lawmakers to block the deal.

Brian Finucane, senior adviser with the US Program at the International Crisis Group, said the sale “sends a vote of confidence to Israel”, even if unintentionally, at a moment when the administration says it wants to calm the region. Analysts see the timing as deliberate on Israel’s part, seeking to lock in expansive US military backing now, wary that a future administration may prove less reliably unconditional.

articles.title: At least 12 dead as Gaza building collapses, many trapped under rubble
articles.summary: Rescue crews in Gaza pull survivors from a collapsed building as cries for help echo beneath the rubble, witnesses say.
articles.body:
At least 12 Palestinians including women and children have died after a multi-storey residential building collapsed overnight in western Gaza City, with six families reportedly trapped underneath, according to local witnesses and journalists.

Gaza’s Civil Defence said on Wednesday at least 12 people died, including five children.

Footage verified by Al Jazeera showed rescue teams pulling young children from the rubble, working alongside residents who dug by hand.

According to witnesses and the verified footage, children’s cries for help could be heard from beneath the concrete as civil defence crews struggled to reach those buried inside.

Another video showed a young girl pulled alive from the wreckage, and several survivors emerging from the rubble, including young children appearing breathless, before being taken away by ambulance.

Local media reported the building had previously been struck in an earlier Israeli bombing, which left it cracked and structurally unsound before it collapsed.

Thousands of homes and apartment buildings damaged or partially destroyed during the war remain uninhabitable across Gaza and at risk of sudden collapse.

Many Palestinians are living in makeshift shelters and half-destroyed, previously bombed buildings across the territory, after Israel restricted the entry of construction materials needed for repairs, as well as the heavy equipment civil defence teams need to safely clear rubble and carry out rescues.

The shortage has left rescue crews relying largely on manual labour to reach people trapped in similar collapses, slowing response times in emergencies.

articles.title: “I sacrificed relationships for a decade”: Ranveer Allahbadia reveals what he gave up during his most intense years of chasing success
articles.summary: Work & Career News: Ranveer Allahbadia has opened up about a part of his career that success stories rarely linger on: the relationships he says he lost while building hi.
articles.body: Ranveer Allahbadia has opened up about a part of his career that success stories rarely linger on: the relationships he says he lost while building his professional life. In a recent social media post, the entrepreneur and podcaster reflected on spending most of his twenties working six-day weeks, eventually moving to seven-day weeks, while people around him warned that he was pushing himself too far.He admits that some friendships were lost along the way.But his reflection is not simply a warning against working hard. Instead, Allahbadia argues that the intense period served the particular goals he was pursuing at the time, while acknowledging that it came with a cost.Read the post hereThat distinction raises a more uncomfortable question about ambition: when does sacrifice become a conscious choice, and when do we simply convince ourselves that everything we are giving up is necessary?Modern work culture often celebrates the visible side of ambition: longer hours, rapid growth, packed calendars, constant productivity and the ability to keep going when everyone else stops.A late night at the office can mean missing dinner with family. A weekend spent working can mean skipping a friend's birthday. Constantly postponing plans can eventually change a friendship even when nobody has a dramatic falling-out.And unlike a missed deadline, these losses may not announce themselves immediately.This is what makes Allahbadia's reflection particularly striking. He does not describe his younger self as someone who accidentally became busy. He describes a period in which he made decisions knowing that they were costing him something.Is sacrifice always a bad thing?People routinely make temporary sacrifices for goals: studying for an exam, building a company, training for a sport or saving money for a major life decision. The question is less about whether sacrifice exists and more about whether the person making it understands what is being traded and for how long.Psychologists have long distinguished between pursuing a goal because it genuinely matters to you and pursuing it because you feel pressured to prove yourself. The first can provide a sense of purpose; the second can make it much harder to recognise when the cost has become unsustainable.That is why Allahbadia's question to people in their “intense years” is more complicated than simply asking whether they work too much.It asks them to identify the trade.The question behind Allahbadia's postThe most revealing part of his message may therefore not be the seven-day workweek.It is his admission that the outcome did not come free.That is a very different way of talking about success. For someone currently working late nights and sacrificing weekends for a future they hope will eventually arrive, that may be the question worth asking:If you know what your ambition is giving you, do you also know what it is taking away?Because sometimes the most important part of a career decision is not the goal you are chasing. articles.title: How retailers in the south of England are fighting back against shoplifting
articles.summary: Shopkeepers tell the BBC why they are turning to social media to name and shame shoplifters.
articles.body:
Disposable barbeques worth £120 gone in seconds. Piles of chocolate bars grabbed. A small child in a balaclava, fleeing with fruit.

As Erdogan Yigitoglu scrolls through his videos, he points out some of the most shocking examples of shoplifting he has captured on his CCTV, some of which he has posted online.

For six years, the Bournemouth convenience shop owner has seen social media as his most effective weapon in his fight against shoplifters, an issue he says loses him thousands of pounds every year.

Yigitoglu has run his shop for 19 years, and he credits publicly shaming and banning shoplifters for a reduction in crime over the past few years.

"Shoplifters damage the business, the environment, country," he says.

"They're stealing from your pocket, my pocket, everybody's pocket.

"If I [do] not sell this item, I can't pay the tax."

He estimates that 40-50% of the people who he says are shoplifting in his posted videos return to pay for the items. Many now avoid his shop entirely, he adds.

He says he only posts when its clear-cut, obvious theft.

Customers support his approach. One young shopper enthusiastically tells Yigitoglu he "liked" the video he had posted the night before.

They are popular too, with the social media posts occasionally getting hundreds of thousands or even millions of views.

Yigitoglu says he understands the impact his videos can have and that some shoplifters have told him the clips have been seen by their workplaces.

He says he will remove a video if he feels the person is truly apologetic and offers a "good excuse".

But his message to shoplifters is clear: "We're always watching, recording and we're always sharing."

Gareth Kimbrey, who runs Setley Ridge Farm Shop in Hampshire, also turned to social media when his shop was targeted.

In April this year, about £400 worth of steak was stolen from his New Forest store.

He posted pictures of the CCTV - which shows two women walking out the back door with armfuls of meat, straight into a getaway car - on the shop's social media accounts and says the video got a "huge response".

He says local people identified the suspects, allowing him to pass on their names and addresses to police.

Kimbrey adds: "I know possibly some people say it's wrong, that we shouldn't put their faces up. But at the end of the day, it isn't a victimless crime.

"If it gets people caught, then it's a really good thing to do."

Two women are due to appear at Southampton Magistrates' Court later this year to face shoplifting charges related to the Setley Ridge incident.

The case is in the minority, as official data shows that only one in five shoplifting offences in 2025-26 led to a charge or summons, and the British Retail Consortium says it remains an under-reported crime.

Yigitoglu says he used to report incidents to the police, but now thinks his time is better spent uploading the videos.

Dorset Police says it has introduced new systems that have simplified the reporting of shoplifting and sped up investigations.

It says where stores support police action, its positive outcome rate is more than double the national average.

The force encourages all retailers to use the online reporting system so it can build cases against prolific offenders.

Policing Minister Sarah Jones says shoplifting was a "pernicious crime that for too long has gone unpunished".

"They need to know that they are going to be punished for what they have done," she adds.

The government says it is exploring other avenues of tackling prolific shoplifting - in addition to prison sentences and drug treatment - such as technology or court orders preventing offenders from visiting certain shops or areas.

articles.title: News helicopter crash in Los Angeles kills three, injures one
articles.summary: NBC Los Angeles helicopter crashes while covering deadly metro bus collision from the air.
articles.body:
A television news helicopter has crashed in Los Angeles while covering a traffic collision, killing at least three people, including one person on the ground.

A fourth person has been taken to the hospital, according to the Los Angeles Fire Department.

The helicopter, belonging to NBC Los Angeles (KNBC-TV), had been providing aerial coverage of a deadly crash between a metro bus and another vehicle.

The helicopter, confirmed by NBC Los Angeles as NewsChopper4, crashed between two commercial buildings in Chatsworth, Los Angeles.

Authorities have not yet released details about the victims.

The live broadcast by the crew captured the moments leading up to the crash. An alert-like sound can be heard shortly before the helicopter begins to descend, after which the live broadcast cuts off.

A spokesperson for the Los Angeles Fire Department said the helicopter crashed into a car park, striking some parked vehicles. Four cars and two storage containers were damaged, but the fire did not spread to any buildings.

The department said more than 50 firefighters responded to the incident and completely extinguished the fire.

Video clips of the scene show the helicopter engulfed in flames after the crash as firefighters worked to control the fire.

The circumstances surrounding the crash remain under investigation. The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration are expected to examine the accident.

articles.title: Onchan residents cite traffic, tourism, and economy as key issues
articles.summary: Residents and business owners in Onchan discuss key concerns ahead of the House of Keys election.
articles.body:
Residents and business owners in Onchan have said traffic, tourism and the cost of living are among their key concerns ahead of the 2026 House of Keys election.

The constituency has the second largest population on the Isle of Man after Douglas, and sits along the east coast.

Sally Hellwich, who runs a family travel business, has lived in Onchan for 30 years. She said she had 'lived, worked, and breathed Onchan" and was "sad" no candidates had considered tourism as a priority.

She said: "I truly believe that tourism underpins the Isle of Man. And if we don't have tourists, we're not generating income for the economy."

As a mother, she added that housing was another big concern for younger generations.

She said: "There's not enough access to housing," adding: "Trying to get on the housing ladder now is just ridiculous."

For Onchan mum Lara, speeding traffic through the town is a big worry, especially with children walking to school on their own.

A rollout of more 20mph zones around the island, including near schools and residential areas, began under the previous administration.

The all-island scheme started in Port Erin in 2025 after Tynwald unanimously voted in 2020 to support speed reductions in urban areas.

Expanding further north, the locations were opposed by residents concerned about congestion.

Lara also welcomed the introduction of more 20mph zones and said she could not understand why "there was so much resistance to it."

She added that in cities like Belfast there are commonly "speed bumps on the road around schools, but they don't have any of that" on the island.

Meanwhile, for Onchan business owners Dinko Matevski and Liliya Slavova, the cost of living was their biggest worry.

Originally from Bulgaria, they have lived on the island for more than 14 years and have run a cafe in the town's Village Walk area for the last three.

Matevski said rising stock prices were "crazy", adding that "every day our suppliers are coming with new prices and we're trying to survive".

Slavova said: "We want to have staff, but we cannot afford it."

In the past three years she noticed a change in customer habits too, with people cutting back their orders.

The Isle of Man House of Keys election takes place on 24 September, with polling stations around the island open from 08:00 to 20:00 BST.

articles.title: Everything we know about Oasis's return to Knebworth
articles.summary: What you need to know about ticket prices, how to avoid traffic and what will happen on the day.
articles.body:
After years of speculation, Oasis are returning to Knebworth House, the scene of their now-legendary 1996 concerts.

They played to 250,000 people across two nights, but the shows have since built a legacy far beyond those who were there.

That became clear to me earlier this year on the Tokyo subway, nearly 6,000 miles (9,660km) away, where I saw a young Japanese fan wearing a T-shirt featuring Liam Gallagher and the words "Oasis Knebworth 1996".

The band must be aware of how important those shows were - the trailer for next year's tour ends with aerial shots slowly revealing their return to the Hertfordshire venue.

So, when Oasis return for four shows in September 2027, how much will tickets cost, who will support them and how can fans get there?

Tickets for Oasis's 1996 Knebworth shows cost just £22.50, while the cheapest tickets for Liam Gallagher's solo concerts there in 2022 were closer to £70.

In 2027 general admission tickets at Knebworth will set you back £170.50, while front standing space costs £203.50.

The venue is one of the more expensive stops on the tour, with tickets for destinations with seating available, such as Manchester's Etihad Stadium and Glasgow's Celtic Park starting at £74.60 and £71.50 respectively.

VIP packages, costing between £317.50 and £513.50, offer benefits including access to a post-show hospitality area, exclusive merchandise or a reserved seating area.

Parking is not included, with prices due to be announced in the coming days.

To buy tickets fans have to sign up with an email address and answer a trivia question to prove they are a fan.

Those who register for shows in the UK may receive a link to buy tickets across Friday 25, Saturday 26 and Sunday 27 September.

After Robbie Williams' shows in 2003, some fans reportedly spent about five hours leaving the car park because of traffic on the nearby A1.

Similar complaints followed Queen's final concert with Freddie Mercury in 1986 and Liam Gallagher's return in 2022 .

For the 2027 shows, Ticketmaster has told fans not to drive and to consider other travel options instead.

Those who do drive have been warned they could face delays getting in and out of the venue.

Hertfordshire Police added it was "working closely with the event promoters and partner agencies to help ensure a safe and enjoyable event for all attendees".

Ticketmaster has said trains would run from Stevenage to London for two hours after each concert, with single tickets costing £10.

As Stevenage station is two miles (3.2km) from Knebworth, a "stewarded, well-lit pedestrianised path" will connect it with the venue, with the walk expected to take about 55 minutes.

Although North Herts Council has said it has not seen a traffic management plan yet, it said it "will be working with the promoter and the Safety Advisory Group on plans in the coming months".

Coach packages will be available to take fans from 124 locations across England and Wales to Knebworth and return them after the concerts finish.

Those with tickets for Saturday night shows can camp the night before and after for £60 per person, which includes parking, in an attempt to ease congestion.

There will be late night bars for campers, and Friday night entertainment will also be provided.

Although gates are expected to open at 14:00 BST, the only confirmed support act so far is former Verve frontman Richard Ashcroft.

He's no stranger to the band as Ashcroft supported the band on their 2025 tour and will appear at all 37 shows in 2027, including the Hertfordshire finale.

In 1996 Noel Gallagher dedicated Cast No Shadow to him during Oasis's second Knebworth show.

Oasis were also joined that year by The Charlatans, Manic Street Preachers, The Prodigy, Cast, The Chemical Brothers, Kula Shaker and tribute band The Bootleg Beatles.

Neil Harrison, who then performed as John Lennon and now manages the band, said it was "hugely flattering" to be invited but remembers feeling nervous before the now-legendary shows.

He said: "We had no idea how we, as a theatre-style act wearing wigs and costumes and playing Beatle songs, would go down. As it happened, rather well.

"Of course, we'd be absolutely delighted to open the show again, and with a new line-up, we haven't aged a bit. We await the call."

articles.title: Cadbury drama turns Stafford into Victorian Birmingham
articles.summary: Film crews arrive in Stafford town centre to shoot scenes for the period drama The Cadburys.
articles.body:
Chocolate giant Cadbury's origins are being brought to the screen in a new TV drama that has turned part of a Midlands town into Victorian Birmingham.

The Cadburys follows brothers Richard and George Cadbury as they try to rescue their family's failing cocoa business before creating one of the world's best-known confectionery brands.

The six-part series stars Toby Regbo as Richard, Harry Gilby as George and Jessica Barden as their sister Maria.

Martin Street and St Martins Place in Stafford have been transformed for filming, with production crews using the town's historic streets to recreate scenes from 1860s Birmingham.

Hannah Farrell, of production company Fable Pictures, said she was "thrilled" with the location and described Stafford as "somewhat of a hidden gem".

"It has so much potential and we feel privileged to be able to showcase the historical town onscreen," she added.

The drama, inspired by Deborah Cadbury's book Chocolate Wars, tells the story of how the Cadbury family sought to turn around their struggling cocoa business in Bournville, Birmingham.

Producers say it will reflect rivalries, family relationships and ambition helping shape the company that would become a household name.

Keith Harrison, from Stafford's Gatehouse Theatre, said about 100 extras were expected to use the venue during filming.

"I think it's a great location for any sort of filming," he said.

"Particularly something from a Victorian era because we've got the buildings, the settings for it.

"It doesn't need that much turning around really to turn it into something authentic."

He said the production could help raise Stafford's profile and encourage more filmmakers to use the area.

"It's a beautiful town and the more we can spread that out, it will help tourism, it will help business, it will help the economy in Stafford."

Staffordshire County Council leader Martin Murray said it was "amazing" to welcome the production to the town and it could boost its profile as well as bring jobs to the area.

The Cadburys is being produced by Fable Pictures for streaming service U and will also be available on BritBox in the US. The series is due to launch in 2027.

articles.title: Stourport man plans 24-hour barefoot Snowdon challenge for charity
articles.summary: Josh Mantle says people think he is "crazy" for wanting to climb Mount Snowdon barefoot.
articles.body:
A man from Worcestershire is planning to climb up and down Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) as many times as possible in 24 hours, completely barefoot.

Josh Mantle, from Stourport, will begin the challenge at 01:00 BST on 11 October and has described it as the "hardest challenge of [his] life", but says it is all in aid of KEMP Hospice.

The 20-year-old said he was inspired by another barefoot climber he met on Wales' tallest mountain, which "lit something inside" him.

"I thought that looks crazy," he said, adding, "and me being the crazy person that I am, I thought I would give that a go."

Mantle is aiming to complete at least three ascents and descents of the mountain in Gwynedd, although a fourth "would be absolutely amazing".

To prepare, he has been conditioning his feet with rubbing alcohol to strengthen his soles.

He added: "I'm also going over Mount Snowdon a lot on my own, and I'm training with weight on my back.

"When I'm doing it on the day without any weight and my friends will be there supporting and carrying all the bags, it should feel a lot easier."

The challenge comes after two knee operations, with a third planned following an ACL injury sustained while skiing.

Mantle said: "People think I'm pretty crazy, and it's safe to say they think I'm mad, but my friends and family know what I'm like; I like a challenge.

"I'm looking forward to it. I wanted to see what I'm capable of and if my knees hold up and I'm able to do this, then I'm sure I'm capable of anything."

Despite the physical demands, Mantle believes his biggest battle will be mental.

"But I'll be focused on the end goal, why I'm there, and that's raising funds for a great charity.

"What they go through is a lot worse than what I'll be going through on the day, and that's what is driving me.

"My feet hurting for a few days is nothing compared to what some people go through."

He developed an affinity for KEMP Hospice, based in the Wyre Forest, after visiting the charity as a schoolboy.

Mantle's original fundraising target was £500, but he has already raised £1,500 and has now increased his goal to £2,000.

articles.title: Shoplifters carrying lists, says Shropshire M&S manager
articles.summary: The Marks and Spencer area manager for Shropshire says shoplifting is a "really large issue".
articles.body:
Shoplifters walk into branches of Marks & Spencer with a list in an attempt to get away with hauls worth thousands of pounds, a regional manager says.

Elisa Lewis, who is responsible for M&S shops in Shropshire, said shoplifting was a "really large issue" and could be "a daily, possibly even hourly, occurrence".

"In my experience it can be anybody," she said. "It can be a bored housewife who's just nicking a jacket for a bit of fun, and the people who we do catch are sometimes those we least expect."

Some shoplifters were people experiencing alcohol or drug dependence who said they were "just doing it to survive".

As a physically smaller woman, she said she found tackling some of them "intimidating", but had become more hardened to it through experience.

Figures collected by the BBC show a slight fall in the number of shoplifting offences across England and Wales in the past financial year and that was mirrored in the West Mercia police force area.

Marks and Spencer has a policy of issuing lifetime bans to shoplifters, which Lewis said could be a big deterrent and a big shock, especially to younger offenders.

But she said sometimes it turned out to be a genuine accident and they took people to their in-house detention room to try to understand their motivations before acting.

In some cases it is no accident though, and she said: "They've come in with a special order, and they go around stealing to order, and that can go into thousands of pounds depending on what people are asking for."

She said the run up to Christmas was always a peak time for shoplifting, with people wanting presents and money.

She also said the quieter times of the day tended to be the peak hours.

"Usually you find in your first hour of trade is where you get people who are reliant on money, drugs, etc," she said.

"They will head for your meat, your alcohol, your suits, because that's what they'll get the most money for."

Lewis said she had seen the level of shoplifting increase and decrease in line with the cost of living, but added: "When there is a presence in the town, they are deterred."

Insp Ingrid Tozer, the West Mercia Police officer responsible for Shrewsbury town centre, said an increased police presence there was making a difference.

Since October there have been six police officers and a sergeant based in the town, and she said incidents of shoplifting had fallen.

"The feedback has been fantastic," she said, and the force believed it had issued criminal behaviour orders to the most prolific offenders.

But engaging traders has been a challenge.

PC Joseph Bradley, one of the police officers based in Shrewsbury, said: "We spent quite a bit of time trying to encourage the shops to report thefts into us.

"We went through a period when we weren't necessarily getting a lot of reports in."

He has worked in the town for 16 years and said he had spent a lot of time building up relationships with traders to make that happen.

That was backed up by Cath Harmer from Shrewsbury BID - a group that represents businesses in the town.

She is the Safer Shrewsbury coordinator, responsible for the Shrewsbury Rangers - a security team which patrols the streets, assisting shopkeepers and the police.

Harmer said: "There is a tendency for retailers to absorb that theft rather than reporting it," and added she wanted to make sure they continued reporting crime.

articles.title: Cheshire brass band trumpets 14th win as Britain's best
articles.summary: Foden's Band, known as one of the world's best brass bands, adds another title to its collection.
articles.body:
A 124-year-old brass band known for being one of the best in the world has won its 14th British title.

Foden's Band came out on top at the 172nd British Open Brass Band Championship, held at the Symphony Hall in Birmingham on Saturday.

It was the latest accolade won by the group, from Sandbach, Cheshire, which has often been at the top of the world rankings since it formed in 1902.

"We're over the moon; the band played fantastic," said Mark Wilkinson, the manager and principal cornet player.

The win added another trophy to Foden's collection, which includes 16 National Championships of Great Britain titles and seven Brass in Concert victories.

Conductor Russell Gray said the band's success took a lot of practice, and it did not "happen by itself".

"The dedication these musicians put into the craft is phenomenal," he told BBC Radio Stoke.

"I'm always in awe that they actually hold down day jobs as well and then come into the band room in the evening to play so magnificently."

Despite all the pressure and hard work that goes into playing "at the highest level", Gray said it was important to remember that it was still a "hobby".

But he added: "You choose to do a hobby; you don't choose to do it badly, do you? You don't go fishing to not catch a fish."

Foden's victory at the British Open, which featured 19 bands, meant it would be invited to represent England at the European Championships in 2028.

Wilkinson, who also won best cornet player at Saturday's contest, said he still got "extremely nervous", not least because of the band's legacy.

"We're the custodians," he added, "so we want to do a fantastic job just like the players before us so we can pass on this legacy to the next generation."

articles.title: Blind artist creates Braille portrait of boxer Lewis Williams
articles.summary: A portrait of Warwickshire heavyweight boxer and Commonwealth Games champion Lewis Williams is made up of 8,000 dots.
articles.body:
A blind artist has created a portrait of heavyweight boxer Lewis Williams completely out of Braille.

Clarke Reynolds, also known as Mr Dot, spent three months creating the artwork of Williams winning his gold Commonwealth Games medal using more than 8,000 dots.

Reynolds, from Havant in Hampshire, said: "Just like any boxer building up for a fight, you have to put the hours in, the training. It took me three months to do; that's over 100 hours."

Williams, from Leamington Spa in Warwickshire, said the portrait was "really special".

"It's reading a lot, of not just my life, but what was going on in the tournament whilst I was boxing there," Williams said.

"It has my name throughout it; you can see the skill and time that's been put in it as well."

Meeting Williams to show him the portrait, Reynolds joked: "I hope it looks like you, because I can't see it, remember."

Reynolds has gradually been losing his sight since he was six years old and has been using Braille as an art form for around eight years.

As his career evolved, he created the persona Mr Dot when he started going into schools to teach children about Braille.

The artist created the portrait, which he said was the first of its kind, to help raise money for the hospice that cared for Williams's dad during the final weeks of his life.

"I say they're like angels that swept into my house on the last few weeks of my dad's life; they swept in and helped my mum out with the care," Williams said.

"I picked them and thought they've done a great job with my family. . . why not try and help?"

Reynolds added: "It has a legacy; Lewis has got big plans for it. If there's anything an artist can do to help, hopefully it raises lots of money."

Williams has plans for the future of the artwork, which includes putting it on show.

"I think it's a bit too much detail; it shouldn't be in one person's house," he told the BBC.

"Even if someone bought it. I don't think it should be for one person.

"It should be on show for other people that are blind that can actually read the Braille and see the whole story to it. I can only see the picture, but there's actually a lot more behind it."

articles.title: Seoul court orders North Korea to pay $32.5m for blowing up office
articles.summary: Pyongyang blew up the Inter-Korean Liaison Office building in June 2020 after days of rising tensions.
articles.body:
A court in Seoul has ordered Pyongyang to pay roughly $32.5m for blowing up an office in North Korea in 2020 that was intended to foster better relations between the two neighbours.

“The court has ruled the North should pay the South Korean government 44.6 billion won in damages,” a spokeswoman for the Seoul Central District Court told the AFP news agency on Wednesday.

The lawsuit over the destruction of the Inter-Korean Liaison Office marks the first time the South Korean government has sought damages directly from the North Korean state, media reports said.

The office building was constructed in the dormant Kaesong Industrial Complex, where South Korean companies once employed North Korean workers.

However, Pyongyang blew up the building in June 2020 after days of rising tensions when activists in the South sent balloons carrying anti-Pyongyang leaflets across the border, with the North denouncing the office as “useless”.

South Korea said it would “review the necessary follow-up measures”, though experts consider it unlikely that Pyongyang would ever pay damages over the demolition of the building in the North Korean city of Kaesong.

The case was filed in 2023 under the government of then-South Korean leader Yoon Suk-yeol, who took a hard line on North Korea before he was ousted following his disastrous martial law declaration.

The office opened in September 2018, days before then-South Korean President Moon Jae-in travelled to Pyongyang for his third summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

About 20 officials from each side were stationed at the office in the following months until operations were suspended in January 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Inter-Korean relations reached a high point in 2018, when Moon and Kim held three summits. But ties deteriorated after a meeting between Kim and United States President Donald Trump in Hanoi, Vietnam, collapsed in February 2019.

articles.title: Tom Phillips: New Zealand apologies to children forced to live in bush for years with fugitive dad
articles.summary: A public inquiry has found that agencies "missed key opportunities" to recover the children sooner.
articles.body:
New Zealand has apologised to the three children of Tom Phillips who vanished with their father for years until he died in a police shootout after an inquiry found authorities failed to protect them.

"There were missed opportunities... and we're sorry about the impact that it's had on those children," Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said on Wednesday.

Agencies involved had "underplayed, minimised or overlooked" how the significant periods of isolation harmed the children, the inquiry found.

When Phillips took his kids, then aged five, seven and eight, into the bush in December 2021, it wasn't the first time he had disappeared with them. Yet they would not be found for almost four years .

Police did not initially launch a search and rescue operation because of a "misconceived view that there were no concerns for the children's welfare", according to the inquiry's findings published on Tuesday.

Former High Court justice Simon Moore, who authored the report, was the sole member of the inquiry.

The report also criticised various agencies involved for "often minimising" concerns raised by the children's mother, which include concerns around firearm safety, "as being part of a parenting dispute".

Phillips died in a shootout with police on 7 September 2025 in the small town of Piopio in New Zealand's North Island. The three children have been under the care of authorities since.

Police later released photographs of what they believe to be one of many squalid campsites where Phillips hid with his children, showing a stash of firearms, ammunition and cans of beer surrounded by dense vegetation.

Phillips' case has gripped New Zealand since the day he disappeared. It has also prompted public outrage as to how a fugitive father, who had three children with him, could have evaded authorities for so long.

Among the "missed opportunities" the inquiry identified were a handful of reported sightings of Phillips and his children during their years of disappearance, which agencies could have more promptly followed up on.

Through interviews with Phillips' family members, among others, the inquiry found that he was not completely cut off from the outside world.

For instance, he visited his mother without the children in February 2022, during which she handed him NZ$1,000 ($575; £426) in cash and food.

He also managed to move through the community during an hours-long shopping trip in August 2023 where he visited various businesses in the Waikato region.

He spent nearly NZ$6,000 in a single day on a haul of goods which include food, children's clothing, gardening supplies, fishing gear, knives and lighters, among other things, the inquiry found.

The inquiry also said the agencies involved – the police, the national child protection agency Oranga Tamariki, the defence force and the ministry of education – could have communicated and coordinated more with each other to better protect the children's welfare.

On Wednesday, Luxon also apologised to the children's mother, acknowledging that they were "let down through this process that spent four years in the bush".

Apart from the prime minister, other government representatives have also apologised and accepted the inquiry's findings.

"To the Phillips children directly, this report has found that our agencies did not take all practical steps to protect you. For that we are deeply sorry," Social Development Minister Louise Upton said on Tuesday.

Upton acknowledged how the children spent four years "in squalid conditions which deprived them of... a happy and healthy childhood".

Deputy Police Commissioner Jill Rogers acknowledged the police's failings but said the investigators involved in the case had "put [in] their hearts and souls".

"Did it take too long? Did we miss opportunities? Yes, we did. You know, you can't unsee the images of where those children were living in those campsites... It's heart-breaking," Rogers told Breakfast, a talk show produced by local news service 1News.

She went on to say: "We have to be better in this. But at the end of the day, our responsibility was to recover the children, and that is what we did."

articles.title: Pakistan ministers warn of energy crisis; Shehbaz government struggles as fuel prices break records
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Pakistan is facing a widening energy crunch as disruptions around key Gulf shipping routes push up global oil prices, fuel costs surge and the governm.
articles.body: Pakistan is facing a widening energy crunch as disruptions around key Gulf shipping routes push up global oil prices, fuel costs surge and the government weighs measures to curb petroleum consumption.Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s government is facing pressure on multiple fronts, with ministers warning about the impact of disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab El-Mandeb while trying to shield consumers from soaring fuel prices.Petrol prices were raised by PKR 4.10 per litre and high-speed diesel by PKR 6.41 per litre on Tuesday night, taking petrol to PKR 384.34 per litre and HSD to PKR 415.83 per litre.The sharp increases have raised concerns about how long Pakistan can absorb the impact of the global oil shock, with climate change minister Musadik Malik saying the government was trying to absorb part of the increase through its fuel relief scheme.Under the scheme, motorcyclists would receive subsidised petrol for up to five litres a week, while car owners would get relief on up to 10 litres every 10 days. Malik said the assistance would not fully offset the increase in fuel prices but represented the maximum burden the economy could currently absorb.Energy minister Awais Leghari also sounded the alarm over the supply situation, saying Pakistan had managed to keep its power plants running despite disruptions by maximising the use of domestic energy resources.In August, 72% of Pakistan’s electricity generation came from domestic sources, including hydropower, local coal, nuclear power, local gas, wind and solar, while 28% came from imported coal and RLNG.Leghari said disruptions to RLNG supplies had pushed spot cargo prices to $23.25 per MMBtu. Increased use of domestic gas for power generation helped Pakistan avoid buying more expensive RLNG, he said.Without the additional domestic gas, Pakistan could have faced another hour of load shedding, while greater reliance on furnace oil or imported RLNG could have increased consumer tariffs by around PKR 10.6 billion, according to the minister.Fuel shock puts Shehbaz government under pressureAs the energy crisis deepens, the government is considering ways to reduce petroleum consumption, including the possibility of a “smart lockdown”.Such measures were used during the peak of the US-Iran war, including a four-day working week and early closure of markets. Information minister Atta Tarar had also indicated that austerity measures could be brought back if the regional situation worsened.However, Malik rejected reports that a smart lockdown was currently being discussed, saying no such discussions had taken place.The government is simultaneously expanding its fuel relief programme. A National Steering Committee on Fuel Subsidy, chaired by deputy prime minister Ishaq Dar, has directed that payments to fuel stations be processed within 24 hours. The scheme, initially piloted in Islamabad, is being rolled out across Pakistan.The fuel shock is also creating political pressure. Jamaat-i-Islami has threatened nationwide demonstrations next week if fuel prices are not reduced.Pakistan has also switched to a daily petroleum pricing mechanism, introduced in July to replace the previous weekly system, as global oil prices became increasingly volatile amid geopolitical tensions.The crisis sharpens as Saudi Arabia has shut its East-West oil pipeline after it came under aerial attack, adding to concerns over global supplies.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
