articles.title: Multiple death sentences in different states are set to be carried out within 24 hours: 'Not very common'
articles.summary: Multiple U.S. executions in the U.S. are set within 24 hours this week, part of a surge that has seen 25 death penalty cases in 2026 with more to come.
articles.body: Multiple executions are scheduled in the U.S. in as many states within a 24-hour window this week. Georgia and Texas had each planned to put a man to death within an hour of each other on Wednesday before a court stepped in to halt the one in Georgia for now, while Alabama is set to carry out another execution the following day. Texas remains scheduled to execute LeJames Norman on Wednesday after a Georgia judge stayed Stacey Humphreys' execution late Tuesday. In the Peach State, 53-year-old Stacey Humphreys was set to be executed on Wednesday for his conviction in the 2003 murders of two real estate agents, 21-year-old Lori Brown and 33-year-old Cindy Williams. But a Cobb County judge stayed his execution late Tuesday, meaning the execution cannot move forward unless the stay is lifted or overturned by a higher court. About an hour after that execution was initially set to happen, Texas scheduled to execute LeJames Norman, 40, for the triple murder of his neighbors during a robbery that turned deadly in 2005. GEORGIA KILLER WHO MURDERED TWO SUBURBAN REAL ESTATE AGENTS FACES EXECUTION AFTER 23-YEAR WAIT FOR JUSTICE Then on Thursday, Alabama plans to execute Jeffery Lee, 50, for a double murder carried out during a 1998 pawn shop holdup. "It's not very common to have this many executions just across a couple of days," Death Penalty Information Center Executive Director Robin Maher told Fox News Digital. "This month, the month of September, we have seven executions scheduled. Last year in October, we had seven executions in a single month. But before then, we'd have to go back all the way to 2010 to see that number in a single month." "Just earlier this year, in August, there were three executions on the same day," she continued. "This is an unusual year in that we're seeing occurrences like a number of executions scheduled on the same day or during the same month. But there's no evidence there's any coordination among the states to have all these executions occur simultaneously. This looks largely to be a coincidence." On Aug. 13, three states — Tennessee, Oklahoma and Alabama — carried out three lethal injections on the same day, marking the first time three states executed prisoners on the same day since January 7, 2010. Weeks earlier, on July 28, Florida carried out two executions in a single day, which was the Sunshine State's first double execution in decades. FLORIDA EXECUTES 74-YEAR-OLD FOR WIFE'S MURDER, BECOMING OLDEST INMATE PUT TO DEATH IN STATE'S MODERN HISTORY In 2026, 25 executions have been carried out in the U.S., and 14 are scheduled for the remainder of the year, although that number could change if courts issue stays or states schedule additional executions. Last year, 11 states carried out 47 executions, making up the most executions carried out in a single year in the U.S. since 2009. Leading the way in executions is Florida, which set a record with 19 inmates put to death in 2025, more than 40% of the U.S. total for the year. It also carried out 15 so far in 2026, accounting for 60% of this year's total across the country. Across 2025 and 2026 thus far, Florida accounts for about 47% of the nation’s executions, as it continues its accelerated pace amid a flurry of death warrants signed by Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis. Texas, Alabama and South Carolina followed Florida, with eight, six and five executions, respectively, in that window. Texas carried out five executions in 2025 and three so far in 2026, Alabama executed five people in 2025 and one in 2026 and South Carolina put five people to death — all in 2025. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Last year was a very unusual year. It was the most executions we've seen in 15 years in the United States," Maher said. "This year, we do not expect to reach that number of executions again. There are a number of other warrants that are still open for this year, but I don't think we'll reach the high that we reached last year." "All of this is really due to Florida," she added. "Gov. DeSantis has decided that he wants to set a record in the number of executions that are conducted during his term. He has scheduled an execution for roughly every two weeks in the state of Florida, both last year and this year." Two executions remain scheduled in Florida for the rest of 2026. Curtis Beasley, 77, is set to be executed Sept. 29 for the 1995 murder of a woman who was bludgeoned with a hammer, while William Lee Thompson, 74, is scheduled for execution Oct. 13 for the 1976 murder of a woman who was beaten, tortured and killed with a chain-link belt.

articles.title: Piddington in Oxfordshire votes to leave UK over asylum plans
articles.summary: Piddington residents vote over proposals to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers nearby.
articles.body:
Residents of an Oxfordshire village have voted to become independent from the UK in a symbolic referendum held in protest at plans to house more than 1,000 migrants at a former military base.

Villagers in Piddington, near Bicester, voted on Tuesday over Home Office proposals to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at nearby MoD Bicester.

The 350 residents were invited to cast their ballot in a small box outside the village hall, the community hub of Piddington.

The referendum was organised by the local parish council and out of 312 votes cast, 285 voted to leave, there were 26 no votes, and one ballot paper was spoiled.

Delivering the result, Susannah Parden, vice chair of the parish council, said: "We are Piddington the village that roars."

Following the result, council chair Tim McNally said: "This is an example of democracy in operation.

"We went into this village hall as the underdogs - we had a plucky idea. We have given a message to the world."

Responding to the village saying it had "roared", Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy told BBC Breakfast: "I think they have – we have heard it, we are listening.

"I do really understand that when changes are made that affect your community it can be very distressing.

"We inherited an enormous asylum backlog, we are processing claims much more quickly, we are removing people who don't have the right to be here," she said.

"Small boat crossing fell this summer for the first time in many years because of the action we have taken.

"While we get a grip on the asylum chaos that we inherited we do need to make sure that we live up to our obligations and house people coming to this country seeking safety."

Tim Beader, Oxfordshire County Council leader, said: "I think what this shows is the Piddington campaigners have done an incredible job to highlight their concerns about the proposed asylum centre.

"It's partially about the proposal itself, and partially about how the government has gone about this without engaging with the local community or looking at the feasibility of this site.

"It's the wrong site for the local communities, for the asylum seekers themselves, and for the taxpayer."

The Home Office announced the plans in June as part of wider proposals to move migrants out of hotels.

Known as "Site A", MoD Bicester is located between the villages of Piddington and Upper and Lower Arncott.

In 2005 it was the target of similar plans for an asylum seekers accommodation centre , which were abandoned by the then-Labour government.

This year's announcement sparked widespread criticism, including from the district council and human rights groups, with many residents expressing shock.

Piddington falls within the constituency of Lib Dem MP for Bicester, Calum Miller. He previously said the plans had been "veiled in secrecy" and that the process did not guarantee public participation "beyond a narrow list of statutory bodies".

However, earlier this month the government published an Urgent Crown Development application .

Miller called it a "clear win for local democracy and for every resident who refused to be shut out of a decision with profound consequences for our communities".

A public consultation on the plans is now running until midnight on 17 September.

articles.title: Smoke from Indonesia’s worst wildfires in years is spreading across Southeast Asia
articles.summary: Indonesian housewife Mimi Marlina rode a motorbike through thickening haze blanketing the city of Pontianak on Borneo island, making a foray to buy groceries and supplies as the Southeast Asian nation battles raging forest fires.
articles.body: PONTIANAK, Indonesia — Indonesian housewife Mimi Marlina rode a motorbike through thickening haze blanketing the city of Pontianak on Borneo island, making a foray to buy groceries and supplies as the Southeast Asian nation battles raging forest fires. “We can still hold it off with medicines, but I’m concerned that if this persists, it will lead to worse illnesses,” said the masked 45-year-old mother of two children who are battling respiratory problems, from coughing and sore throats to fever. The province of West Kalimantan on Borneo, home to Pontianak, is one of the areas worst hit by Indonesia’s most intense wildfires in 11 years as “super-El Niño” weather conditions drive up temperatures and cause punishing droughts. Despite wearing a mask, Mimi said she herself was laboring for breath in the widespread haze and pollution spikes, which often push air quality to hazardous levels. Volunteers are going door-to-door in the province, handing out cylinders of life-giving oxygen to residents and firefighters struggling to breathe, in a campaign called “Rumah Oksigen,” or Oxygen House. The air has also turned unhealthy in neighboring Singapore and Malaysia because of the transboundary smog, often called haze in Southeast Asia’s humid weather, for a mix of smoke from clearing land for farming, soot and tiny suspended particles. “Visits for respiratory illness cases are on the rise due to the fires,” said Popong Solihat, head of a public health clinic in Pontianak. More than 12.5 million people have been exposed to haze caused by fires across seven provinces on Indonesia’s islands of Borneo and Sumatra, health ministry data shows. The numbers battling wildfire-related respiratory illnesses in those provinces had more than doubled to 113,336 by Sept. 9, versus 50,891 on Sept. 1. In the first 11 days of September, Solihat’s clinic treated 187 cases of breathing difficulties, compared with 422 for all of August. “And the daily visits now could range between 80 and 120,” he added. Among those who received oxygen cylinders is Suriana in the district of Kubu Raya, who said her health had deteriorated as air quality worsened. “I often feel short of breath when exposed to the smoke,” said the 54-year-old, who like many Indonesians goes by one name. “It seems to be getting worse now, particularly in the mornings and evenings, when the haze is at its strongest.” Indonesia’s emissions of 19.7 million metric tons during the week to Sept. 7 made up more than a third of the global total, according to the Fire Emissions Watch portal of the European Union’s Copernicus climate monitoring service. From January to July this year, fires raged across almost 500,000 acres of land, government data showed. The environmental group YKAN has estimated that fire damaged an additional 1.4 million acres in August. Indonesia has stepped up fire-fighting efforts, sending more than 50 aircraft to drop water on the flames and engage in cloud seeding to bring rain, while Japan sent three CH-47 Chinook and 180 crew last week to help.

articles.title: US charges five people over alleged Russian plots
articles.summary: Prosecutors said that the group worked on behalf of Russian intelligence services to carry out attacks and murders.
articles.body:
Five people have been charged over alleged Russian intelligence-linked plots involving surveillance, recruitment and planned killings, according to an indictment unsealed by the United States Department of Justice .

Prosecutors said on Tuesday that the group worked on behalf of Russian intelligence services to carry out attacks and murders internationally, including within the US, and that all five remain at large.

The defendants were identified as Russian national Yuri Khrameev, 63, his son Kirill Khrameev, 27, Cubans Oemis Romagoza Durruthy and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, both 35, and 22-year-old Venezuelan Angel Eduardo Castro.

All five were charged with conspiring to finance terrorism, while Khrameev, Suarez and Castro face additional charges of conspiring to commit murder for hire.

At a news conference, Attorney General Todd Blanche said the plots included attempts to kill a Russian dissident believed to be living in the Washington, DC area.

Justice Department officials said the network had recruited several people in the US to carry out surveillance on Russian dissidents, targeting individuals both domestically and in Lithuania.

In one instance, a recruit was reportedly promised $40,000 to make a US-based target “disappear”. A separate recruit was allegedly offered $25,000 the previous year to kill someone in Lithuania.

Russia’s embassy in the US has not commented on the case. Moscow has consistently rejected accusations that it has orchestrated assassination operations on foreign soil, including in the US.

articles.title: In 2011, a man opened his late great-aunt’s Virginia closet and found 345 comics; the collection including Batman comics sold for about $3.5 million
articles.summary: US News: A remarkable discovery in Martinsville, Virginia, highlights the unearthing of a significant comic book collection worth $3.5 million, showcasing Golden Age comics including the famous Batman debut. Read on to explore the fascinating story behind this rare find and its impact on the collectibles market.
articles.body: Michael Rorrer, a 31-year-old Oxnard, California, resident, discovered 345 comics in a basement closet in his late great-aunt's Martinsville, Virginia, home in 2011, a collection quietly assembled decades earlier by his great-uncle Billy Wright. According to the Associated Press, Wright, who died in 1994 at age 66, collected the comics as a boy and young man between 1936 and 1941, later becoming a chemical engineer, and never discussed the collection with relatives beyond one brief mention. Heritage Auctions described the find as one of the most important Golden Age comic book collections in decades. Heritage Auctions reported in February 2012 that 44 of the 345 comics in Wright's collection ranked among the top 100 Golden Age comics in the Overstreet Comic Book Price Guide, a detail the Associated Press also cited in its coverage of the auction. That concentration of high-value issues is part of what convinced buyers and experts of the collection's authenticity.Paper quality from that era makes surviving copies unusually fragileComics from this era were printed on cheap, highly acidic wood-pulp newsprint, since publishers considered them disposable at the time. Research published in Polymer Degradation and Stability has shown that volatile organic compounds emitted by paper and archival materials continue to degrade them even in protective storage, which helps explain why so few Golden Age comics survive in good condition.Detective Comics No. 27 led the sale at $522,813As per AP (23 Feb., 2012) via Hurriyet Daily News, Heritage Auctions' sale of Billy Wright's Detective Comics #27 for nearly $523,000 is the highest selling price of this item in the New York auction of February 2012. In this regard, the first issue of Superman from the year 1938 called Action Comics No. 1 fetched a price of $298,750. Heritage Auctions (Feb. 2012) said Billy Wright’s copy of Batman #1 sold for $274,850 at the New York auction.The Antique Trader (February 18, 2025) reports that a Near Mint copy of Captain America Comics #2 (Timely, 1941) sold through Heritage Auctions for $113,500. This was close to the $113,525 that Wright's own copy of the same issue fetched at the original 2012 sale. A 2012 hedonic pricing study in the Journal of Cultural Economics, based on 1,100 American collectible comic books, found that a comic's condition, rarity, and documented ownership history each measurably affect its sale price, separate from the story or character inside; one reason collections with a clear, verified history like Wright's tend to command strong prices.The total sale brought in about $3.5 millionAssociated Press (Feb. 2012) stated that the Billy Wright comic book collection found by Michael Rorrer was auctioned off for around $3.5 million at Heritage Auctions' February 2012 auction, with the money split between Rorrer, his brother Jonathan, and his mother Lisa Hernandez. According to Lon Allen, the managing director of comic books at Heritage Auctions, this was a type of Golden Age comic book collection that everybody thought did not exist anymore.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
